$comment: #1951 — THE ONE DISCOVER CARD-ADMISSION DECISION.
Ruling 021: when two consumers must agree about the same input, the unit to
share is the DECISION, not the ingredient. A shared predicate under two
policies is still two policies — and three implementations that merely AGREE
are still three policies that can drift apart on any given Tuesday.
This rule has three implementations because it has to: it runs in TypeScript
on web, in Swift on native, and in Python inside the Flow Sentinel's
dark-class detector. No import can span those. So the shared unit is this
table — the decision, expressed as data — and every implementation's test
drives ITS predicate through EVERY row here. A row is a claim about the RULE,
never about one surface.
WHAT WENT WRONG WITHOUT IT. `feed_item_is_renderable` shipped in UX-P092 as a
third copy nobody had enumerated, carrying the PRE-#1935 reading on two arms.
It feeds the dark-class limb — the #1935-family detector — so a predicate more
permissive than the clients made the family it hunts invisible: seven
golferless-whathit tournaments, 100% dark on both surfaces, scored
`7 built, 7 renderable`. A PASS over a dark tier. Cycle 90 corrected the
reading; this file removes the ability to drift again unnoticed.
TO ADD AN ARM: add rows here FIRST, watch all three suites go red, then fix
the implementations. To add a card TYPE: add it to `emitted_types` and give it
rows, or `registry` fails the build — an emitted type with no arm is dark by
construction, which is #1935 restated as a build error.
$unconditional_comment: A type with no well-formed suppression row. Declared rather than tolerated,
because the coverage guard's job is to refuse a type that is pinned in only
one direction — a type with only admitted rows is satisfied by `return true`,
and a type with only suppressed rows is satisfied by `return false`, which
would 'detect' perfectly and starve the feed. `event` is genuinely
unconditional on all three surfaces (a real matchup plus a status/score is
never a bare tile), so the exception is real; naming it here keeps it
checkable. A declared unconditional type must STILL carry a
malformed-envelope suppression row, so `return true` remains insufficient.

why_not_executed: jest is a deploy gate here and the Swift test target is not reachable from
CI, so native is asserted against SOURCE in the same file that executes the
other two. That buys less than execution and it is what is available — a
source assertion that runs on every push beats an execution assertion that
runs on an iOS lane's laptop.

note: Returns a bool, not a reason code, and that asymmetry is deliberate: the
reason codes are web's suppression TELEMETRY, while the sentinel only needs
the verdict. The shared unit is the decision (admit / drop), so a row's
`expected_reason: null` reads as True here and any string reads as False.

$cases_comment: WELL-FORMED items only carry an `expected_reason`. Malformed-ENVELOPE rows
(`data` absent, `data` a list, the item not an object at all) are marked
`malformed_envelope: true`: every implementation must still fall closed on
them, and the reason STRING is not part of the shared decision because native
never sees such a payload — its decoder rejects it before the predicate runs.
Malformed LEADER rows are ordinary rows, because a leader object is decoded
content that both erased-type surfaces genuinely face (gotcha #23).

THE ORDER PIN. 'Settled means settled' — a card with a result leads with the result and must never fall back to a probability that is now history. The server never sends both, so this row pins the ORDER of the two arms rather than a live case, which is precisely the kind of invariant that rots silently.

The erased-type failure mode. Native writes `leader != nil` and that is COMPLETE there, because its decoder rejects a malformed leader first. TypeScript and Python have no such gate and `{}` is truthy, so a presence test written 'to match native' matches the source and not the behaviour.
A nameless leader cannot be printed.
The card prints `probability * 100`; without one there is no percentage.
A numeric-looking string is not a number on either erased-type surface.
Gotcha #23 — an independent-binary field can sum past 100%, so a leader reading over 1.0 is corrupt rather than confident.

A bundle earns its slot on any member that can render.
A bundle of bare tiles is a bare tile with a header.
An empty list has no renderable member.

Bundles are not expected to nest, but a malformed deep chain must never blow the stack — and BOTH surfaces cut at depth > 3, so WHERE they cut is part of the shared decision rather than an implementation detail. Note precisely where: the guard lives inside the BUNDLE arm, so it counts nested bundles and never gates a leaf. The first draft of this row nested four bundles and expected a cut; both implementations admitted it, agreeing with each other and disagreeing with the row — which is the table doing its job on its own author. Five bundles put a BUNDLE at depth 4, and that is the one that is cut; the renderable concept beneath it is unreachable on every surface.

Fail closed — an unrecognised type is dropped, never shown bare. This is also how a NEW card type behaves on the day it ships without arms, which is why `registry` fails the build for an emitted type with no rows.

A card whose `data` never arrived. Web read `item.data` unguarded until #1951 and THREW here — inside a render-path `.filter()`, which blanks the whole Discover page (#1909's class). Falling closed is the stated property of this predicate, and throwing is not falling closed.

The `event` arm is the one unconditional admit on all three surfaces, so it is the arm most likely to be reached with nothing behind it. Python's envelope guard sits BEFORE its type dispatch and suppressed this; web's `case "event": return null` sat before any envelope check and admitted it. Both now guard the envelope first — an event card with no matchup, status or score behind it is not 'always renderable', it is not a card.
Same shape, arriving as the wrong JSON container.
